newsitem.title: USA: Oklahoma agency rules in favor of SBC.
newsitem.headline: Oklahoma agency rules in favor of SBC.

text.p: The three-member Oklahoma Corporation Commission on Friday backed SBC Communications Inc's application to provide long-distance phone service for customers in the state.
"It was a 2-1 vote to uphold Bell," OCC spokesman Pat Petree told Reuters by telephone from Oklahoma City.
Petree said the OCC, the state's top phone regulator, would forward its decision to the Federal Communications Commission, which has final say in the matter, by May 1.
If approved by the FCC, SBC would be the first Baby Bell allowed to enter the $80 billion long-distance business.

The company's bid appeared to suffer a setback last week when an Oklahoma administrative law judge recommended that the carrier's request be rejected because it had not met a federal checklist for entry. But the OCC ruled in favor of SBC during a public meeting on Friday morning.

SBC's application had been opposed by AT&T Corp, Sprint Corp, MCI Communications, Brooks Fiber Properties Inc and Oklahoma's attorney general, among others, who argued that SBC had not yet opened its local telephone monopoly to competitors.
Under the 1996 communications law, SBC and other regional Bells must meet a 14-point checklist showing they had opened their local monopolies before gaining FCC approval for long-distance services.
Robert Lynch, general counsel for external affairs for SBC's Southwestern Bell unit, welcomed the OCC's ruling.

"It is very significant, very important ...They have now said there is sufficient compliance (by SBC) with the federal law so the FCC should now do its part, which is to open long-distance markets to the same kind of competition."
He also defended SBC's record in allowing in competition.
"The company is offering everything these competitors need to provide local service. Whether they are taking advantage of all this was not what was being decided (by the OCC)."
He said he expected the FCC to scrutinize SBC's request "very carefully" but added that he "like to think they'll see this application in the same way as the OCC did."
